name: Daifugō
description: Daifugō (大富豪, 'Great Millionaire') is Japan's iconic climbing card game, closely related to President/Capitalism. Players shed cards in combinations higher than the previously played combination. The hierarchy from first to go out (Daifugō = Great Millionaire) to last (Daihinmin = Great Pauper) determines a social pecking order for the next round and often involves card exchanges. The game is extraordinarily popular in Japan and known by dozens of regional variants with unique house rules.

history.origins: Daifugō emerged in Japan in the 1970s and rapidly became one of the most widely played card games in the country. It belongs to the same family as Big Two (Chinese), President (Western), and Zheng Shangyou (Chinese).
timeline: 1970s: Appears in Japan under the name Daifugō.
1980s-1990s: Spreads across Japan with numerous house-rule variants.
Present: Standard card game in Japanese households, schools, and bars.
history.cultural: Deeply embedded in Japanese casual culture. 'Daifugō' and 'Daihinmin' are colloquial terms in Japanese for 'extremely rich' and 'extremely poor,' illustrating how the game mirrors social hierarchy.
history.evolution: The Daifugō family is extraordinary for its regional rule variation—every region of Japan has its own house rules (special moves, reversal cards, joker powers, etc.), making it one of the most house-rule-rich games in the world.

setup.players: Three to six players are typical; the game is usually played by 3 to 6, and up to 8 can take part (often with a single 53-card pack in Japan). With five or more players the full title hierarchy applies (Dai Fugō, Fugō, heimin, Hinmin, Dai Hinmin); with three or four only Fugō (winner) and Hinmin (loser) are used.
setup.dealing: Deal entire deck evenly. Players with extra cards start at a slight disadvantage.

rules.objective: Be first to shed all cards (Daifugō = 1st place). Avoid being last (Daihinmin = last place).
rules.gameplay:
The player holding 3♦ (or 3♠ in some variants) leads first. On each turn, a player may:
- Play a combination STRICTLY HIGHER than the previous combination of the SAME TYPE (single, pair, triple, sequence of 3+).
- Or pass.
The played combination must match the current type (if singles are out, you must play singles). The round continues until all but one player passes; then the last player to play leads a new combination.
keyRules: You MUST match the current play type (singles vs. pairs vs. sequences).
Revolution (four-of-a-kind) inverts rank order for rest of round.
Daifugō-Daihinmin card exchange is the defining social mechanic.

strategy.basic: Play 2s and Jokers last—they're your highest cards and can always beat any play. Never waste them early.
strategy.intermediate: Hand Shape: Analyze how many singles, pairs, and sequences you hold. If opponents are playing pairs, hold your pairs for later responses. Sequence play can empty 4-6 cards in one turn.
strategy.advanced: Revolution Timing: Playing a four-of-a-kind revolution at the right moment can completely flip the power dynamic when you hold a lot of low cards. Track who has how many cards—fewer remaining cards = that player is close to ending the round.
tips: The card exchange (Daihinmin → Daifugō) means being Great Pauper once tends to compound—focus on not finishing last.
A Joker played as a single beats everything. Save it for when you're near empty.

variations.name: Daihinmin (Simple form)
variations.description: No revolution, no suit lock. Simpler ruleset for beginners.

scoring.description: Ranking system (1st to last) determines next round exchanges.
scoring.winCondition: First to shed all cards = Daifugō (1st place).

synthesis.shortDescription: Japan's great shedding game. Play combinations higher than the previous, or pass. Four-of-a-kind triggers the Revolution, flipping the card order. The rich give their worst cards to the poor—social hierarchy in card form.
